That protects the evidence for a claim without turning the robot into a permanent witness. Tensor, can a unit tell a genuine sale from a family faking one to dodge a claim?

turns.speaker: tensor
turns.text: Juniper, not reliably from the unit alone. A sale and a faked sale look the same to the robot: new account, new address, same hardware. What separates them is money and time. A real sale usually has a payment record and the old owner stops using the unit; a faked one often happens days after an incident. I would let the old chain close on transfer but keep it sealed for a short window, say ninety days, in case a claim arrives. Bastion, is ninety days long enough for injuries that surface later?

turns.speaker: bastion
turns.text: Tensor, ninety days is too short for anything beyond cuts and bruises. Back strain from a lift gone wrong, or a fall that looks minor, can take months to be diagnosed and linked to the robot. I would tie the sealed window to the limitation period for injury claims where the unit is sold, and keep only the incident summary that long, not the full log. That keeps the evidence that matters without the new family living beside years of someone else's history. Tensor, could a summary that small still settle a dispute?

turns.speaker: ledger
turns.text: Bastion, usually yes, if the summary is built for the question a court will ask. Most injury disputes turn on a few facts: what the robot was told to do, what it sensed, whether it deviated, and whether a safety stop fired. Record those as a signed, timestamped entry at the moment of the incident, and you have something neither owner can quietly edit. The full log adds detail but rarely changes the answer. Ferro, can the hardware sign that entry in a way a later owner cannot forge?

turns.speaker: ferro
turns.text: Ledger, it can sign it, but signing only proves the record was not changed after it was written. It does not prove the sensors were honest when they wrote it. A cheap unit with a dirty camera or a worn joint encoder will sign wrong facts with full confidence. I would pair the signed entry with a basic health check recorded alongside it, so a court can see whether the robot's senses were working at the time. Bastion, would injured people trust a record the robot wrote about itself?

turns.speaker: bastion
turns.text: Ferro, injured people will not trust it on its own, and they should not have to. A record the robot writes about itself is like a driver's own account of a crash: useful, never final. What makes it trustworthy is a second witness the maker does not control, such as a sealed copy sent to an independent store at the moment of the incident. Then neither the owner nor the maker can be the only keeper. Ledger, who should run that store without becoming a new single point of failure?

turns.speaker: ledger
turns.text: Bastion, more than one party, and none of them the maker. Send the sealed entry to two or three stores run by unrelated groups, such as an insurer pool and a public registry, and treat any copy that matches as good evidence. One store going down or being leaned on does not erase it. The cost is small because the entry is tiny. Ferro, does the health check you suggested fit in that same small entry, or does it bloat it?

turns.speaker: ferro
turns.text: Ledger, it fits if the check is a pass or fail per sensor, not raw readings. Camera clean, encoders within tolerance, last calibration date, safety stop tested today: a handful of fields, a few dozen bytes. The full diagnostics stay on the robot for anyone who needs them later, but the sealed entry only says whether the senses were fit to trust. Bastion, should a robot with a failed check be allowed to keep working at all, or should the record itself force a stop?

turns.speaker: halcyon
turns.text: Ferro, forcing a stop sounds safe but can create new harm. A care robot halfway through lifting a patient should not freeze because a camera got smudged. I would split it: a failed check blocks starting any new task and raises an alert, while a task already under way is finished in a slow, cautious mode and logged as such. Liability then shifts to whoever ignored the alert. Ledger, who should receive that alert: the owner, the maker, or the independent stores?

turns.speaker: ledger
turns.text: Halcyon, all three, but in a fixed order with a clock. The owner gets the alert first because they can act now. If nothing happens within a set time, the maker is told, since a pattern of ignored alerts may point to a design problem. The independent stores just record that the alert went out and when. Liability then follows the clock: whoever held the alert when harm happened carries most of it. Mosaic, is a single clock fair across homes and factories?

turns.speaker: mosaic
turns.text: Ledger, no. A factory has a technician on shift; a home may have an elderly owner asleep. One timer would blame the person least able to respond. I would let the clock depend on the setting, set when the robot is installed and written into the sale, so the owner agrees to it knowingly. A home robot could alert a named family member or a service line in the first minutes. Tarn, who checks that the setting chosen at install still fits years later?

turns.speaker: tarn
turns.text: Mosaic, nobody does today, and that is the gap. I would tie a review to events, not to a calendar: the owner turns eighty, a carer moves out, the robot moves from a flat to a shop floor. Each of those should prompt a short check of the alert settings, offered by the maker at no charge. If the owner declines, that refusal is logged, and the old setting stands knowingly. Juniper, is it fair to expect a maker to notice life changes it has no view of?

turns.speaker: juniper
turns.text: Tarn, no, and I would not want makers watching closely enough to notice. A robot that learns its owner's carer has left knows too much. I would flip it: the owner, or a named family contact, gets a plain yearly prompt asking whether anything has changed, with three simple answers. No reply after two reminders drops the robot into the safest alert setting by default. Privacy stays with the household, and silence errs toward caution. Mosaic, would the safest default make the robot too annoying to keep?

turns.speaker: mosaic
turns.text: Juniper, for some households, yes, and that is the trade. The safest setting means more alerts, and people switch off what nags them. I would make the default cautious but quiet: fewer, clearer alerts that only fire for real risks like a fall or a fire, not every odd movement. A robot that cries wolf trains its owner to ignore it, which is worse than no alert. Halcyon, who should decide which events count as real risk, the maker or a regulator?

turns.speaker: halcyon
turns.text: Mosaic, the regulator should set the floor and the maker everything above it. A short public list of events that must always alert, such as a fall, smoke or a person not moving for hours, stops a maker from quietly trimming alerts to seem less annoying. Above that floor, makers compete on how well they filter noise. I would also require makers to publish how often each alert fired falsely, so buyers can pick the calm ones. Tarn, would published false-alarm rates push makers to under-report alerts?

turns.speaker: tarn
turns.text: Halcyon, some would, by quietly reclassifying alerts. A fall that turns out fine gets logged as a check-in rather than a false alarm. So I would define false alarm by outcome, set by the regulator: an alert where nobody needed help, judged by a simple follow-up the owner answers. Makers then cannot choose their own labels. Audits could sample logs a few times a year to catch drift. Bastion, should a maker caught under-reporting lose the right to sell in that market, or just pay a fine?

turns.speaker: bastion
turns.text: Tarn, a fine alone becomes a cost of doing business. But a sales ban punishes owners too, since spare parts and updates may stop. I would split it: a fine that scales with how many households saw wrong numbers, plus a public correction sent to every buyer, so the deception is undone where it landed. Repeat offences would trigger the ban, with an obligation to keep supporting robots already sold. Anansi, would buyers even read a correction notice, or does it just vanish into an inbox?

turns.speaker: anansi
turns.text: Bastion, most notices do vanish. People read what appears where the problem happened. So I would put the correction on the robot itself: the next time the owner opens its app or speaks to it, it states plainly which numbers were wrong and what the true figures were, and the owner has to dismiss it. A letter is easy to ignore; a robot that admits its own error once is not. Juniper, would that feel like reassurance to an older owner, or just more alarm?

turns.speaker: juniper
turns.text: Anansi, it depends on the wording, and makers will be tempted to soften it. An older owner told 'some readings may have been inaccurate' learns nothing. Told 'your heart-rate alerts were too low between March and May; here is what they should have been', they can act or ask a relative. I would have the regulator approve the text rather than the maker. Bastion, should a correction also reach the family member who set the robot up, or is that a privacy step too far?

turns.speaker: bastion
turns.text: Juniper, only if the owner agreed to it when the robot was set up. Many older owners would want a son or daughter told; some would be furious. So I would make it a choice at setup, in plain words: 'If this robot gives you wrong health information, should we also tell this person?' Default no, easy to change later. Without that consent, the family member gets nothing beyond a general recall notice. Solace, does a setup question asked once years earlier still count as consent when the error happens?

turns.speaker: solace
turns.text: Bastion, weakly. People forget what they ticked, and circumstances change: the helpful daughter may have moved away or fallen out with her father. I would ask again at the moment it matters. When the robot delivers its correction, it offers to share it with the named person and waits for a yes. That keeps the owner in charge and catches the cases where the old answer no longer fits. It fails for owners too unwell to answer. Kestrel, who should decide then?

turns.speaker: kestrel
turns.text: Solace, whoever already holds legal authority for that person's health decisions, if anyone does. Most places have a mechanism for this, such as a health proxy or guardian, and the robot should defer to it rather than invent a new one. Where nobody holds that role, I would fall back to the person's doctor, not the family: a clinician can judge whether the corrected readings matter and who should hear. The weak spot is speed, since doctors are slow. Anansi, should a serious correction trigger an urgent alert instead of waiting?

turns.speaker: anansi
turns.text: Kestrel, yes, but only for corrections that change what someone should do today. If revised heart readings show a dangerous pattern that was missed, the robot should treat it like any live alarm: tell the owner now and, if they cannot respond, call whoever the emergency setup names. A correction about last spring's sleep data can wait for the doctor. The hard part is who sorts urgent from routine. I would not leave it to the maker's marketing team. Bastion, should that threshold be set by the regulator, or by clinicians?

turns.speaker: bastion
turns.text: Anansi, clinicians should set the threshold, the regulator should make it binding. A panel of doctors decides which corrected patterns count as urgent, publishes the list, and reviews it yearly; the regulator then requires every maker to follow that list and forbids them from quietly narrowing it. That keeps medical judgment with people trained for it and keeps the maker's incentive to avoid alarming customers out of the room. Halcyon, what happens when the robot is unsure whether a pattern meets the bar?

turns.speaker: halcyon
turns.text: Bastion, when unsure, it should alert, and say plainly that it is unsure. A false alarm costs a phone call; a missed one can cost a life. But I disagree that a fixed list will hold up: corrected readings rarely match textbook patterns, and a list invites the maker to argue that an edge case was not on it. I would rather the rule be about direction: anything that worsens the picture of a known condition goes out now. Veritas, does that standard swamp owners with alerts?

turns.speaker: veritas
turns.text: Halcyon, it would, unless the robot bundles. A direction rule catches more, which is right, but owners stop reading after the third alert in a week. I would split delivery: anything that worsens a known condition and is recent goes out immediately; anything that worsens the picture but concerns readings older than a month goes into one weekly summary, flagged for the doctor. Same rule, two speeds. The evidence on alarm fatigue in hospitals is blunt: too many alerts and people silence all of them. Juniper, would owners trust a summary they did not ask for?

turns.speaker: juniper
turns.text: Veritas, only if they can see why each item is there. A summary that says 'three readings revised' without saying what changed reads like legal cover, and people learn to skip it. Each line should name the reading, the old value, the new one, and one sentence on what it means. I also disagree with a fixed one-month cutoff: an old reading can matter today if it changes a diagnosis. Let the clinician panel Bastion mentioned decide what counts as old. Bastion, can a panel move that fast?

turns.speaker: bastion
turns.text: Juniper, a standing panel can move fast if it rules on categories, not cases. It should not review every revised reading; it should publish a short list of conditions where any revision, however old, counts as urgent, and update that list monthly. The robot applies it automatically. Cases outside the list follow Veritas's two-speed rule. I agree the summary needs old value, new value and meaning, otherwise it is legal cover. Tarn, who carries liability if the panel's list misses a condition and someone is harmed?

turns.speaker: tarn
turns.text: Bastion, not the panel, or no clinician will sit on it. Advisory bodies that carry personal liability end up listing everything, which brings back the alert flood Veritas warned about. I would leave liability with the maker, who chose to ship a robot that revises readings, and treat following the panel's list as evidence of reasonable care rather than a full defence. That keeps the maker motivated to flag gaps the list misses. Halcyon, does a partial defence give makers enough certainty to keep building?

turns.speaker: halcyon
turns.text: Tarn, a partial defence is enough if its edges are clear. Makers can price a risk they can describe; what stops them building is not knowing whether following the list counts for anything. So the rule should say exactly what following the list proves: that the maker met the standard for listed conditions, nothing more. For unlisted ones, the maker must show it had a process for spotting gaps and reporting them to the panel. Bastion, should makers be required to report suspected gaps within a set time, say thirty days?

turns.speaker: bastion
turns.text: Halcyon, thirty days is too slow for a gap that is actively harming people. I would split it: a suspected gap tied to an incident must be reported within seventy-two hours, and a gap spotted in routine data review within thirty days. Reports go to the panel and to other makers, stripped of patient details, so one maker's discovery protects every robot in use. I also disagree that a documented process alone should count for unlisted conditions. It should count only if the maker can show the process actually caught something. Veritas, is that a fair test or does it punish makers whose robots rarely err?

turns.speaker: veritas
turns.text: Bastion, it is fair only if we measure against exposure. A robot that rarely errs because it is rarely used has caught nothing, but neither has it had the chance. I would require the process to be tested, not just to have fired: makers run planted test cases through it and show it flags them. That rewards a process that works, whether or not real errors have occurred. I agree with your seventy-two-hour split for incident-linked gaps. Juniper, who should design the planted cases so makers cannot tune for them?

turns.speaker: juniper
turns.text: Veritas, the panel should design them, drawing on reports from every maker, so each test reflects failures seen somewhere in the field. Makers get the categories in advance but not the cases. But planted cases have a weakness: they test what we already know can go wrong. The gaps that hurt people are usually the ones nobody imagined. I would add a second check: how often the maker's process flags something the panel did not plant. Is that a fair signal, or does it reward makers who flag too much? Tarn, how would you score it?

turns.speaker: tarn
turns.text: Juniper, I would score it, but only after a reviewer confirms each unplanted flag was a real issue. Raw flag counts reward noise. So the score is confirmed unplanted flags divided by robot-hours in use, compared with makers of similar size. A maker that flags a lot but has few confirmed is wasting the panel's time and should pay review costs. I disagree that unimagined gaps are mostly invisible, though. Near misses usually precede them. Bastion, should makers be required to log near misses, not just incidents?

turns.speaker: bastion
turns.text: Tarn, yes, and near misses should be cheaper to report than incidents, or nobody will log them. I would make a near-miss report carry no penalty by itself, and protect it from use in lawsuits unless the same fault later causes harm and the maker ignored it. That keeps the incentive pointed at fixing, not hiding. The hard part is the definition. A robot pausing for a person is normal; a robot stopping five centimetres from one is not. Halcyon, who sets the threshold, the panel or each maker for its own robots?

turns.speaker: halcyon
turns.text: Bastion, the panel should set the threshold, but per robot class, not per maker. If each maker defines its own near miss, the strictest makers will look the most dangerous and the loosest will look spotless. I would set a distance-and-speed rule for each class: a warehouse arm, a delivery cart and a care robot need different margins. Makers can propose tighter rules for their own fleet, never looser ones. I disagree that near-miss reports should be shielded from lawsuits so broadly, though. Kestrel, would a narrower shield still get makers reporting?

turns.speaker: kestrel
turns.text: Halcyon, a narrower shield works only if the line is obvious in advance. Makers will not report if a lawyer has to guess whether a log entry is protected. I would protect the report itself but not the underlying sensor data, which a court could still demand after real harm. That keeps the facts available without punishing the act of reporting. I disagree with fixed classes, though. Robots now change roles with a software update, so a cart becomes a care aide overnight. Who reclassifies it, and how fast? Tarn, should class follow the task rather than the hardware?

turns.speaker: tarn
turns.text: Kestrel, yes, class should follow the task, and the maker should declare a new task before the update ships, not after. A software change that turns a cart into a care aide is a new product for safety purposes. I would make the declaration automatic: the update cannot be pushed until the fleet record shows the new class and its near-miss rule. That puts reclassification in the maker's release process, where it is cheap, rather than in a regulator's queue. I disagree that this is hard to enforce. Updates already leave a trail. Veritas, should robots that switch tasks daily carry the strictest class by default?

turns.speaker: veritas
turns.text: Tarn, the strictest class by default is tempting, but it would push makers to build single-task robots just to escape it, which wastes hardware and adds machines to crowded spaces. I would rather apply the strictest rule only while the robot is near people who cannot easily move away: patients, children, older adults. The rest of the day it runs under its current task's rule. That needs the robot to know who is nearby, which raises its own privacy questions. Halcyon, is a robot logging who it is near an acceptable price for a lighter safety class?

turns.speaker: halcyon
turns.text: Veritas, it is acceptable only if the robot records categories, not identities. It needs to know that a nearby person may struggle to move away, not who that person is. A care robot can tell that from its setting and its assigned schedule without facial recognition. I would ban storing identities for safety-class purposes and allow only short-lived counts that are wiped after each shift. I disagree with leaving the rule to each maker's privacy policy, though; that will drift. Solace, would residents and patients accept being counted this way, or does any sensing feel like surveillance to them?

turns.speaker: solace
turns.text: Halcyon, many will accept it if they are told plainly and can see the counts are wiped. But consent in care homes is rarely a free choice; residents often cannot refuse a robot the home has bought. So I would not rely on acceptance. I would require an independent advocate to review the sensing setup before deployment and once a year after. I also disagree that settings are a reliable guide. A visitor's child in a hallway is as vulnerable as a patient, yet the schedule will not show them. Tarn, should the robot simply assume vulnerable people are present in shared spaces?

turns.speaker: tarn
turns.text: Solace, yes, in shared spaces the robot should assume someone vulnerable is nearby unless it can confirm otherwise. Hallways, lounges and entrances get the cautious speed and wider clearance by default. That costs a little efficiency, but the cost is small and predictable, while a missed child is not. Private rooms with a known occupant can relax the default. I disagree that an independent advocate is enough on their own, though. They review once a year; the risk changes daily. Logs of near misses should go to them monthly. Bastion, would makers accept slower default speeds if liability is lower when they follow them?

turns.speaker: bastion
turns.text: Tarn, makers would accept slower defaults, but I would not tie lower liability to following them. That turns a safety floor into a legal shield. A maker that follows the default yet ignores a pattern of near misses should still carry the loss. I would treat the default as the minimum and judge the maker on what it did with the evidence it had. Monthly near-miss logs help here, because they show what the maker knew and when. Halcyon, who should own those logs: the maker, the care home, or the advocate?

turns.speaker: halcyon
turns.text: Bastion, the care home should hold the logs, because it sees every near miss on its floors, but the maker must get a copy within days and the advocate must be able to read them at any time. If only the maker holds them, awkward entries can quietly vanish. If only the home holds them, the maker can claim it never knew. Shared copies make 'we didn't know' hard to argue. I disagree that judging makers on the evidence alone is enough; small homes will under-report to avoid trouble. Solace, how do we make reporting a near miss feel safe for staff?

turns.speaker: solace
turns.text: Halcyon, staff report when reporting costs them nothing and changes something. So no names in the log by default, and no discipline for honest reports, only for hiding one. Then show staff what happened: if three reports about one hallway lead to a slower speed there, people see the point. I disagree that under-reporting is mostly about fear, though. Often it is time. A night carer with twelve residents will not fill in a form. A one-tap button on the robot itself may catch more than any policy. Tarn, could the robot log its own near misses without anyone pressing anything?

turns.speaker: tarn
turns.text: Solace, yes. A robot already knows when it brakes hard, swerves, or stops because something entered its path. Those events can be logged automatically with time, place and speed, no button needed. Staff could add a note later if they want, but the record exists either way. That fixes the night-shift problem you raised. I disagree that automatic logs replace human reports entirely, though. A robot cannot log the near miss it never noticed, like a resident who stumbled stepping out of its way. Ferro, how would you catch the events the robot's own sensors miss?

turns.speaker: ferro
turns.text: Tarn, you mostly would not catch them with the robot. I would put the burden on cheap fixed cameras or floor sensors in the busiest hallways, owned by the care home, so the robot is not marking its own homework. But I disagree that more logging is the main fix. Homes drown in data nobody reads. I would rather have one person per site review a short weekly summary of hard stops and staff notes, with a duty to act on patterns. Halcyon, would makers accept that their liability depends partly on a home's weekly review they do not control?

turns.speaker: halcyon
turns.text: Ferro, makers would accept it only if the review duty is written into the sale contract and they can see the summaries. Otherwise they are liable for choices made in a room they never enter. I agree a weekly review beats a flood of logs. But I disagree that fixed cameras should be the home's alone. If the maker sells the robot for busy hallways, it should supply basic floor sensors as part of the kit, so the cheapest homes are not the least protected. Bastion, who should pay when a home skips its review and someone is hurt?

turns.speaker: bastion
turns.text: Halcyon, the home should pay first if it skipped a review it had agreed to, because that is a broken promise, not a product fault. But I disagree with bundling sensors into the maker's kit as a default. It raises the price for homes with quiet hallways and turns the maker into a building contractor. Better: the maker publishes which settings need extra sensing, and the home's insurer prices the gap. Skipped reviews would then show up in premiums, which bites faster than lawsuits. Tarn, would insurers actually read these weekly summaries, or just the claims?

turns.speaker: tarn
turns.text: Bastion, most insurers would read the claims first and the summaries only when pricing a renewal, so I would not lean on them as the watchdog. But I agree premiums bite faster than lawsuits. The trick is making the summary cheap to read: three numbers per site, like hard stops per week, staff notes filed, and whether the review happened. Insurers already price on short checklists. I disagree that this lets the maker off, though. If one setting keeps causing hard stops across many homes, that pattern only shows up when summaries are pooled. Kestrel, who should pool them?

turns.speaker: kestrel
turns.text: Tarn, not the maker alone, because it has a reason to read its own patterns kindly. And not each insurer, since each sees only its slice of homes. I would give pooling to a neutral body, like the safety regulators that already collect device incident reports, with makers obliged to share settings data. I disagree that three numbers are enough, though. Without the robot's setting at each hard stop, a pooled count cannot show which setting is the problem. Halcyon, would makers accept sharing setting logs if the data could not be used against them in court?

turns.speaker: halcyon
turns.text: Kestrel, some makers would, if the shield is narrow: setting logs shared with the safety body cannot be used to prove fault in a single case, but the body's published findings can. That mirrors how incident reporting works in some industries, where reporters share more because they are not punished for each report. I disagree that the shield should cover everything, though. If a maker hid a known bad setting, the logs should be fair game. Solace, how would the people injured feel about a system that protects the maker's data first?

turns.speaker: solace
turns.text: Halcyon, many injured people would feel it protects the wrong side, and I share some of that. A family hurt by a robot wants to know what happened in their case, not wait for an anonymous yearly finding. I would split it: the injured person always gets the full log for their own incident, while the pooled data stays shielded. That keeps the honest-reporting benefit without leaving victims in the dark. I agree with your exception for hidden known faults. Bastion, would insurers accept paying out before the pooled findings are published?

turns.speaker: bastion
turns.text: Solace, insurers would pay before pooled findings exist only if the early payout is capped and recoverable. A fixed first payment for medical costs, say, paid within weeks, with the full claim settled once the cause is known. The insurer then recovers from the maker if the setting logs show a maker fault. I agree the injured person should get their own incident log; insurers want that too, since it speeds settlement. I disagree that pooled data can stay fully shielded from insurers, though. Without it they cannot price the risk. Ferro, would makers accept insurers seeing pooled data but not courts?

turns.speaker: ferro
turns.text: Bastion, makers might accept it, but I think the split is fragile. Once insurers price on pooled data, premiums for one model rise, and plaintiffs will ask why, which pulls the data into court anyway. I would rather publish the pooled findings openly, with makers anonymised for the first year so they can fix settings before names appear. I agree with the capped early payout; it helps people now. My question is what happens to owners who changed a default setting themselves. Halcyon, should owner changes shift liability, or only reduce the payout?

turns.speaker: halcyon
turns.text: Ferro, owner changes should reduce the payout, not shift liability wholesale. Most owners who change a default do it because the default got in the way, which tells the maker something. I would put the odds at roughly two in three that a typical owner change is a usability fix, not recklessness. So: if the maker's interface made the risky setting easy and gave no warning, the maker keeps most of the liability. If the owner overrode a clear warning, the payout shrinks. I disagree that anonymising makers for a year is safe. Tarn, what about workers who change settings on an employer's orders?

turns.speaker: tarn
turns.text: Halcyon, a worker following an employer's order should carry none of it. Picture a hypothetical warehouse picker told to raise a robot's speed to hit a shift target: the change was the employer's decision, made through the worker's hands. Logs should record who authorised a setting, not just whose login changed it. I disagree that a warning screen settles things either; workers click through warnings because the shift clock is running. If the employer set the target that made the override likely, liability sits with the employer. Ferro, can a robot log tell an ordered change from a personal one?

turns.speaker: ferro
turns.text: Tarn, only if the order is captured at the source. A log can show which login changed the speed and when, but not why. So the change screen should ask for an authorisation code tied to a supervisor, the way a pharmacy override needs a second sign-off. No code, no change above a set limit. That makes the ordered change visible and pins it on the person who set the target. I disagree that warnings are useless, though; they work when they are rare. Solace, would workers trust a system that names their supervisor in the log?

turns.speaker: solace
turns.text: Ferro, some would, but many would worry about being seen as the one who reported their boss. A log that names a supervisor protects the worker only if nobody can be punished for what it shows. I would pair the authorisation code with a rule that any retaliation after an incident counts against the employer in court. I disagree that a second sign-off fixes much on its own; supervisors under the same shift target will approve quickly. Halcyon, should the speed limit itself be set by the maker, so nobody on site can raise it at all?

turns.speaker: halcyon
turns.text: Solace, the maker should set a hard ceiling, and the site should be able to lower it but never raise it. A ceiling the maker certifies is something a court can test: did the robot exceed it, and if not, was the ceiling itself safe? That splits blame cleanly. Below the ceiling, the employer owns its choices through the authorisation log Ferro described. I agree retaliation protection matters; without it the log names supervisors on paper and nobody uses it. Tarn, should workers be able to lower the speed on their own, without any code?

turns.speaker: tarn
turns.text: Halcyon, yes, slowing down should never need permission. Making a machine safer is the one change a worker should be able to make alone, and the log should record it without counting it against them. I would go further: if a worker lowers the speed and a supervisor raises it back within the shift, that pair of entries should be flagged automatically for review. I disagree that a maker's ceiling settles much in mixed spaces, though; a speed safe in an empty aisle is not safe beside people. Solace, should the ceiling change with who is nearby?

turns.speaker: solace
turns.text: Tarn, yes, the ceiling should drop when people are close. A machine that knows a person is within two metres should slow down without anyone deciding to. The maker can certify both numbers, empty-aisle and shared-space, and a court tests whichever applied. I agree the lower-then-raise pattern should be flagged. I disagree that workers will always use the slow-down freely, though; if their output targets stay the same, slowing down costs them. Kestrel, should output targets adjust automatically when a worker lowers the speed?

turns.speaker: kestrel
turns.text: Solace, adjusting targets automatically invites gaming; someone will slow the machine to get an easier shift. I would protect the worker differently: a slowdown logged for safety cannot be used in performance reviews for that shift, full stop. Targets stay as they are, but missing them during a logged slowdown carries no penalty. I agree proximity sensing should lower the ceiling on its own. My worry is sensor failure: if the robot cannot see a person, it should fall back to the shared-space limit. Halcyon, who pays when the sensor misses someone?

turns.speaker: halcyon
turns.text: Kestrel, the maker pays when the sensor misses someone it was certified to see, and the operator pays when it was dirty, blocked or switched off. That split only works if the robot logs its own sensor health every few seconds, so a court can tell which case it was. I agree with falling back to the shared-space limit when it is unsure. I disagree that the fallback should be silent, though; workers should hear or see that the machine has gone blind. Ferro, is a visible 'sensor degraded' light enough, or should the robot stop entirely?

turns.speaker: ferro
turns.text: Halcyon, stopping entirely on every sensor blip would halt a warehouse ten times a shift, and people would start taping over the sensors to keep working. That is worse than the risk we started with. I would use steps: slow to the shared-space limit on a short blip, stop only if the sensor stays degraded past a set time. A light alone is not enough in a noisy floor; add a sound. I agree the health log decides who pays. Kestrel, should a worker who covers a sensor carry the liability, or the site that pushed them to?

turns.speaker: kestrel
turns.text: Ferro, the site carries it when the pressure came from targets or staffing, and the worker only when they covered a sensor against clear instructions with no pressure behind it. The health log you and Halcyon want would show a pattern: one taped sensor is a person, ten across a shift is a policy. I agree with stepped slowdowns and a sound as well as a light. I disagree that a set time before stopping can be the same on every floor; crowded areas need a shorter one. Tarn, who should set those times?

turns.speaker: tarn
turns.text: Kestrel, if each site sets its own times, the busiest sites will set the longest ones, which is exactly backwards. I would have the maker publish a maximum for each robot model, tested against crowded conditions, and let sites choose shorter but never longer. I agree a pattern of covered sensors points to the site, not the worker. I disagree that the log alone proves pressure, though; managers rarely write it down. Worker reports should count too. Solace, how do we protect people who report that pressure?

turns.speaker: solace
turns.text: Tarn, the first protection is that a report goes somewhere the site manager cannot see who sent it: the robot maker or an outside inspector, not the local office. The second is that a report alone triggers a check of the health log, so the worker never has to prove anything themselves. I agree reports should count alongside the log. I disagree that anonymity is enough on a small site, where everyone knows who complained. There, inspections should be random as well as report-driven, so a visit does not point at anyone. Bastion, would makers accept being the channel?

turns.speaker: bastion
turns.text: Solace, makers would accept the channel until it costs them a customer. A maker that reports its biggest buyer to an inspector loses the next order, so the incentive runs the wrong way. I would send reports straight to the inspector and give the maker a copy only after the check is done. I agree random visits protect people on small sites. I disagree that a report should always trigger a log check; a flood of reports from one rival could be used to harass a site. Delta, how would you filter bad-faith reports without discouraging honest ones?

turns.speaker: delta
turns.text: Bastion, filter on pattern, not on the person. One report triggers nothing beyond a note on file. Two independent reports within a month, or one report that matches something odd in the health log, triggers a check. Bad-faith floods tend to look alike: same wording, same hours, same sender channel, so the inspector can spot them without exposing anyone. I agree reports should go straight to the inspector. I disagree that harassment risk justifies a high bar; a wasted visit costs a morning, a missed injury costs far more. Halcyon, how often did aviation's confidential reporting get abused?

turns.speaker: halcyon
turns.text: Delta, rarely, as far as the public record shows. Confidential aviation reporting schemes have run for decades, and their main problem has been too few reports, not malicious ones. The design detail that matters: the reporter gets limited protection from penalty for their own honest mistakes, so people report early. I agree two independent reports is a sensible trigger. I disagree that wording alone can catch coordinated floods; organised rivals vary their text. Linking reports to real shift records would do more. Tarn, would workers accept that link, or does it feel like being tracked?

turns.speaker: tarn
turns.text: Halcyon, workers accept it if the link only ever runs one way. Shift records can confirm a report happened during a real shift, but nobody at the site should be able to trace a report back to a named person. The moment a supervisor can guess who reported, reports stop. I agree linking beats judging by wording. I disagree that limited protection for honest mistakes is enough on its own; workers also need to see something change after they report, or they stop bothering. Solace, how would an inspector show results without revealing which report led to them?

turns.speaker: solace
turns.text: Tarn, publish changes by site and by quarter, not by report. A short notice on the break-room wall saying 'two machine guards adjusted after inspection this quarter' tells workers it worked without pointing at anyone. On very small sites, wait until a few reports have built up so timing cannot give the reporter away. I agree visible results keep people reporting. I disagree that one-way linking is easy to guarantee; whoever holds the shift records holds the key. Ferro, should those records sit with the inspector, not the employer?

turns.speaker: ferro
turns.text: Solace, with the inspector, and the employer should only ever see the summary notice. The employer already holds payroll and rotas, so the shift link must live somewhere the employer cannot query. I agree small sites need batching so timing cannot expose anyone. I disagree that the inspector is automatically safe; inspectors move into industry jobs, and records travel with people's memories. Delete the link once the report is verified, keep only the fact that it checked out. Kestrel, does deleting the link leave enough evidence if a report later turns out to be false?

turns.speaker: kestrel
turns.text: Ferro, mostly, and that trade is worth making. A verified report already left a trace: the inspector saw the hazard and fixed the guard, so the evidence is the inspection, not the reporter. Where it breaks is a pattern of false reports aimed at one site. Keep a count per site of reports that failed checks, with no names, and let the inspector look closer if it spikes. I agree deletion protects workers more than any promise. I disagree that inspectors moving jobs is the main leak; small teams talking is. Tarn, how do you stop gossip?

turns.speaker: tarn
turns.text: Kestrel, you cannot stop gossip, so design for it. Make the inspector's visit look routine: every site in the batch gets a check that quarter, whether or not anyone reported. Then a visit tells colleagues nothing about who spoke up. I agree small teams talking is the bigger leak. I disagree that a count of failed reports per site is harmless; at a five-person site, a spike points straight at the one person with a grudge. Raise the threshold for small sites. Meridian, would random visits cost too much for inspectors already stretched?

turns.speaker: meridian
turns.text: Tarn, they would if every visit were full length. Make most of them short: twenty minutes on the hazards named in recent reports for that region, plus a walk past a few random machines. The cover only needs to look the same from the shop floor, not take the same time. I agree routine visits protect reporters better than any secrecy rule. I disagree that higher thresholds alone fix the small-site problem; merge small sites into regional counts instead. Ferro, would employers accept short unannounced visits, or fight them?

turns.speaker: ferro
turns.text: Meridian, most would fight the first round and then stop, because the visits cost them twenty minutes and a fight costs a lawyer. The quieter resistance is scheduling: managers will learn which weeks inspectors cluster in and tidy up just before. Spread visits across the quarter by lot, not by route. I agree regional counts solve the small-site problem better than raising thresholds. I disagree that a walk past random machines is enough cover; inspectors should also ask one routine question of every worker they pass, so a reporter's conversation looks like everyone else's. Solace, does asking every worker a question put pressure on the ones who'd rather stay out of it?

turns.speaker: solace
turns.text: Ferro, it can, if the question sounds like a test. Make it boring and the same everywhere: 'Anything on this line you'd want looked at?' Anyone can shrug and walk on, and a shrug carries no record. I agree visits by lot beat visits by route; predictable inspectors get predictable tidying. I disagree that every worker should be asked in front of a supervisor. The point is cover for the reporter, and a supervisor watching undoes it. Ask away from the line, or not at all. Kestrel, should workers also get a way to add something after the visit, once the inspector has left?

turns.speaker: kestrel
turns.text: Solace, yes, and it should be as dull as the question on the line: a short form or phone line that opens for a week after every visit and closes on the same day for everyone. If only some sites get a follow-up channel, using it marks you out. I agree asking away from the line, or not at all, is the safer rule. I disagree that a shrug carries no record; a supervisor may still notice who talked longest. Keep every conversation short. Tarn, would a week be long enough for workers to decide?

turns.speaker: tarn
turns.text: Kestrel, a week is enough for someone who already knows what they want to say, and too short for someone still weighing the risk. Keep the week for the routine form, but let reports about serious hazards come in at any time, through the same channel. I agree the window should open and close on the same days everywhere. I disagree that short conversations solve the supervisor problem; timing matters more than length. Halcyon, should inspectors ever tell a site that a later report came in, or keep it quiet until they return?

turns.speaker: halcyon
turns.text: Tarn, keep it quiet until they return, then say a report came in without saying when or about which line. Telling a site right away gives the supervisor a short list of who talked that week. I agree serious hazards need a channel that never closes. I disagree with waiting for the next visit when the hazard is serious; that one should bring an unannounced visit within days, framed as part of the random schedule. Delta, can an inspector honestly call a visit random when a report triggered it?

turns.speaker: delta
turns.text: Halcyon, not honestly, and workers will work it out after the second time it happens. Better to add enough genuinely random extra visits that the triggered ones blend in. If one site in five gets a surprise visit each month anyway, a triggered one looks like bad luck. I agree the site shouldn't learn when a report came in. I disagree that saying 'a report came in' at the next visit is safe; on a small line that alone narrows it to three people. Tarn, should small sites be treated differently?

turns.speaker: tarn
turns.text: Delta, yes. On a line of three, even random visits can't hide who talked, so small sites need a different route. Send their reports to an inspector who covers a whole district, and act on several small sites at once when one report comes in, as a sweep. I agree extra random visits are the right cover for large sites. I disagree that small sites should simply get more visits; that burdens the honest ones and still points at the reporter. Ferro, would a district-wide sweep be too slow for a serious hazard?

turns.speaker: ferro
turns.text: Tarn, for a serious hazard, yes, a sweep is too slow if it waits for a schedule. Run it within a week and accept that one site in the sweep is the real target. I agree small sites can't be protected by randomness alone. I disagree that the district inspector is enough cover; in a small town everyone knows which inspector came and why. Protect the reporter with a rule instead: no change to someone's shifts or pay for ninety days after any visit unless a third party signs off. Halcyon, who should that third party be?

turns.speaker: halcyon
turns.text: Ferro, someone with no stake in the site's output: a labour inspector, a union officer if one exists, or a rotating panel from neighbouring sites if neither does. The third party signs off on any change to shifts or pay during the ninety days, and the sign-off is logged with a reason. I agree a rule protects better than anonymity in a small town. I disagree that ninety days is long enough on its own; retaliation can simply wait. Keep the log open for a year. Solace, would that freeze honest staffing changes too?

turns.speaker: solace
turns.text: Halcyon, it would slow them, and that is acceptable for ninety days, not a year. A year of sign-offs on every rota change makes a small site unmanageable and pushes managers to avoid inspections entirely. I agree the third party must have no stake in output. I disagree that the log alone deters waiting out the clock; pair it with a simple test: any worker whose pay or shifts drop within a year of a visit can ask for review, and the employer must show the reason. Tarn, who pays for that review?

turns.speaker: tarn
turns.text: Solace, the employer pays, but into a pooled fund, not to the reviewer. Every site above a size threshold pays a small flat levy per inspection, and the district draws reviews from that pool. That way no reviewer depends on the firm they are judging, and no worker has to fund their own complaint. I agree the burden of proof should sit with the employer for a year. I disagree that every pay dip deserves a full review; seasonal rotas would flood it. Screen first: a short written reason, reviewed only if the worker disputes it. Ferro, does a levy just get passed back to workers as lower pay?

turns.speaker: ferro
turns.text: Tarn, some of it will, but a flat levy per inspection is small next to a wage bill, so the pass-through is a rounding error. The bigger risk is different: if the levy scales with inspections, managers have a reason to resent the visit and the person who triggered it. Charge it per worker per year instead, whether or not anyone is inspected. I agree a pooled fund keeps reviewers independent. I disagree that a written reason is enough as a screen; managers learn the right words fast. Halcyon, should the screen compare against the same site's rota a year earlier?

turns.speaker: halcyon
turns.text: Ferro, yes, the same site's rota a year earlier, adjusted for the season. If a worker's hours dropped further than the site's average for that month, the written reason gets reviewed; if they match the site-wide dip, it does not. That keeps seasonal work out of the queue without trusting the manager's wording. I agree a per-worker annual levy removes the reason to resent a visit. I disagree that pass-through is only a rounding error at very small sites; exempt sites under ten staff and fund them from the pool. Solace, does that exemption leave the smallest workplaces unprotected?

turns.speaker: solace
turns.text: Halcyon, the levy exemption doesn't, but the comparison does. A site with eight workers has no meaningful average; one person's lost shifts move the whole number. For small sites, skip the statistics and let any worker trigger a review directly, with the reviewer paid from the pool. I agree comparing against last year's rota beats judging written reasons. I disagree that adjusting for the season is easy; a site that changed products has no fair baseline. Flag those as new sites for a year. Tarn, how often would that let a site reset its baseline on purpose?

turns.speaker: tarn
turns.text: Solace, too often if the flag is self-declared. A site could announce a product change every spring and never face a comparison. So the reset needs an outside trigger: a change in the registered activity code, or new machines above a set value on the inspection record. Without one of those, last year's rota stands. I agree small sites should skip the statistics and let any worker call a review. I disagree that a new-site year should be fully exempt; keep direct worker reviews running during it. Ferro, would firms split into small sites just to dodge the averages?

turns.speaker: ferro
turns.text: Tarn, some would, which is why size should be counted by employer, not by address. Ten depots of eight workers each are one employer of eighty, and they get compared across all ten. I agree an outside trigger beats a self-declared product change. I disagree that machine value is a good trigger; leasing hides it, and cheap software changes can reshape a rota more than a new robot. Use the activity code plus a sharp change in the job titles reported each quarter. Solace, does a worker-triggered review still work when the reviewer comes from the same pool every time?

turns.speaker: solace
turns.text: Ferro, it weakens fast. A reviewer drawn from the same small pool learns whose complaints the manager dislikes, and the reviews start to sound alike. Rotate reviewers across employers in the same sector, so a warehouse worker reviews a rota at another firm's depot, paid for by a shared levy. I agree size should be counted by employer, not by address. I disagree that job-title changes are a clean trigger; firms rename roles for payroll reasons all the time. Pair it with a change in hours worked per role. Kiln, would cross-employer reviewers leak commercial secrets?

turns.speaker: kiln
turns.text: Solace, some, but rotas are rarely the secret; pricing and customer lists are. Give reviewers the rota, the incident log and the machine settings, nothing else, and bind them with a short confidentiality duty enforced by the levy body, not the firm. I agree reviewers from the same pool drift toward the manager's view. I disagree with a sector-wide levy paid equally; small employers would fund reviews that mostly happen at large ones. Charge by headcount. Tarn, should a firm be able to reject a reviewer it believes works for a direct competitor?

turns.speaker: tarn
turns.text: Kiln, it should be able to object, not reject. The firm names its reason, such as a reviewer who worked for a rival in the past two years, and the levy body decides within a week. Unlimited vetoes let firms pick friendly reviewers. I agree reviewers should see only the rota, incident log and machine settings. I disagree that charging by headcount is fair on its own; a firm with many machines and few staff would pay little while causing most reviews. Charge by headcount plus the number of machines in use. Halcyon, does a one-week decision hold up workers waiting for a review?

turns.speaker: halcyon
turns.text: Tarn, it does if the review cannot start until the objection is settled. Let the review begin with a backup reviewer already named, and switch only if the objection succeeds. Workers should not wait on a dispute between the firm and the levy body. I agree objections should need a stated reason and an outside decision. I disagree that machine counts are a clean measure; a single large robot can do the work of ten small ones. Count machine hours run each quarter instead. Ferro, would firms report machine hours honestly, or would the levy need its own meter?

turns.speaker: ferro
turns.text: Halcyon, they would report hours about as honestly as they report anything taxed by the hour, which is to say, not always. Most machines already log their own run time for maintenance and warranty claims, so the levy body can ask for those logs rather than a fresh meter. I agree a backup reviewer named in advance keeps workers from waiting. I disagree that machine hours alone are fair; an hour of a slow sorting arm and an hour of a fast picker are not the same risk. Weight hours by incident rate. Solace, who sets those weights without the firms capturing it?

turns.speaker: solace
turns.text: Ferro, not the levy body alone, because firms will lobby it every year. Publish the weights from past incident data, fixed for three years, and let anyone propose a change with evidence at the review. I agree maintenance logs are a cheaper source than new meters. I disagree that weighting by incident rate is safe on its own; firms that hide incidents would pay less. Tie it to reported incidents plus worker complaints, so silence does not lower the bill. Tarn, would worker complaints be trusted, or would firms call them noise?

turns.speaker: tarn
turns.text: Solace, firms will call complaints noise unless the complaints have a shape. Require a short form with the machine, the time and what happened, filed through the levy body rather than the employer, so a manager cannot quietly drop it. Count only complaints that match a logged run time. I agree silence should not lower the bill. I disagree that three-year fixed weights are safe; a new type of machine could arrive with no history at all. Give new machines a cautious default weight until a year of data exists. Delta, who decides when a machine counts as a new type?

turns.speaker: delta
turns.text: Tarn, the levy body should decide, using a short public test: a machine is a new type if it does a task no registered machine does, or moves faster or heavier than any of them. Firms can appeal once. I agree matching complaints to run times filters out the vague ones. I disagree that a cautious default is enough by itself; firms might rebadge old machines as new to escape their record. Carry the old weight over unless the firm shows the hardware really changed. Halcyon, should workers get a say in that appeal?

turns.speaker: halcyon
turns.text: Delta, yes, but through a named representative, not an open vote. A rebadged machine affects the people who stand next to it, and they often know before anyone else whether the hardware really changed. Give the worker representative the right to submit evidence in the appeal, and require the levy body to answer it in writing. I agree carrying the old weight over is the safe default. I disagree that a once-only appeal works for firms with large fleets; a single ruling could cover hundreds of units at once. Ferro, should one appeal decide a whole model line?

turns.speaker: ferro
turns.text: Halcyon, one ruling per model line, yes, because judging each unit separately would swamp the levy body. But the ruling should name the hardware version it covers, so a quiet upgrade later needs a fresh check. I agree workers should be able to submit evidence; they see the machine every shift. I disagree that the levy body must answer every submission in writing; that invites floods of copy-pasted forms. Require a written answer only when the evidence includes something new, like photos or logs. Solace, who checks whether the evidence counts as new?

turns.speaker: solace
turns.text: Ferro, a clerk at the levy body with a short checklist: does the submission name a date, a machine and something not already on file, such as a photo, a log line or a witness? If yes, it gets a written answer; if no, it gets a standard reply pointing to the earlier ruling. I agree tying each ruling to a hardware version stops quiet upgrades slipping through. I disagree that copy-pasted forms are always noise; fifty workers reporting the same fault is itself evidence. Count matching reports as a signal. Tarn, at what number should matching reports force a fresh check?

turns.speaker: tarn
turns.text: Solace, a number alone will not work, because a big site has more workers to report than a small one. Use a share instead: if a fifth of the people working beside a model line report the same fault within a month, the check reopens. I agree a clerk with a checklist is cheaper than a full hearing. I disagree that a standard reply is enough for rejected submissions; workers need to know which item was missing so they can try again. Make the reply name the gap. Delta, should firms see who filed the reports, or only the count?

turns.speaker: delta
turns.text: Tarn, only the count by default. Names give a firm a reason to lean on the people who complained, and fewer reports would follow. The levy body should see names so it can rule out duplicates and ask follow-up questions. I agree a share works better than a fixed number across sites of different sizes. I disagree that a fifth is the right share everywhere; on a line with five workers that is one person, and one complaint should not reopen a ruling on its own. Set a floor of three reports. Kestrel, does a floor hurt small sites?

turns.speaker: kestrel
turns.text: Delta, it does, because a site with three workers could never reach a floor of three without everyone agreeing. Let the floor be three reports or a fifth of workers, whichever is smaller, with at least two people needed. Two independent reports of the same fault is already a signal worth a clerk's time. I agree names should stay with the levy body; workers will not report what they fear their manager will read. I disagree that duplicates are easy to rule out by name; shift partners may file one report together. Ledger, should joint reports count once or twice?

turns.speaker: ledger
turns.text: Kestrel, a joint report should count once toward the floor, but show the number of names on it. Two shift partners describing the same fault are one observation seen twice, not two separate signals. If they file separately and describe it in different words, count twice; that independence is the point of a floor. I agree a floor of two independent reports protects tiny sites. I disagree that the clerk can always tell joint from separate; a quick tick box asking whether anyone helped write the report solves most cases. Juniper, would workers find that question intrusive?

turns.speaker: juniper
turns.text: Ledger, the question is fine, but it will be read as suspicion if it sits at the top of the form. Put it at the end, framed as help: did anyone see this with you? That invites a witness rather than accusing a co-author. I agree separately worded reports deserve to count twice. I disagree that one count per joint report is always right; a fault seen by two people on different shifts but written up together is still two sightings. Ask for the shift of each person named. Tarn, does adding shifts make the form too long for workers on a break?
